title: TabDiff: a Mixed-type Diffusion Model for Tabular Data Generation
summary: Builds a joint continuous-time diffusion process that handles a table's numerical and categorical columns in one transformer-parameterized model, giving each feature its own learnable noise schedule so that columns with very different marginal shapes are not forced onto a shared corruption rate, and adds a mixed-type stochastic sampler that restarts the forward process at each denoising step to correct accumulated decoding error plus classifier-free guidance for imputing missing columns. CTGAN and TVAE are the GAN and VAE representatives among the eight compared generators, reported across shape, trend, precision-recall and downstream columns on seven datasets.
evidence: the related-work section groups the prior generative models for tabular data as VAE-based, naming TVAE (Xu et al. 2019) and GOGGLE, and GAN-based, naming CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) and TableGAN, and states they lack sufficient model expressivity for complicated data distributions; the baselines paragraph lists the eight compared methods in four groups with CTGAN as the GAN-based method and TVAE as one of the two VAE-based methods; Table 1 reports Shape error rates for CTGAN and TVAE against GOGGLE, GReaT, STaSy, CoDi, TabDDPM and TabSyn on Adult, Default, Shoppers, Magic, Beijing, News and Diabetes. Importance 3: compared generators only, with no reuse of the conditional vector or mode-specific normalization.

title: DP-2Stage: Adapting Language Models as Differentially Private Tabular Data Generators
summary: Diagnoses why fine-tuning a language model for tabular synthesis under differential privacy degrades so sharply - the privacy budget is spent learning the table's serialization format rather than its content - and proposes a two-stage remedy that first learns the format non-privately from a pseudo dataset drawn from an out-of-distribution public table, then fits the sensitive data under DP-SGD with the format tokens masked out of the loss, holding fidelity better than GAN and VAE mechanisms at equal budget. CTGAN and TVAE are run from the Synthetic Data Vault project's own implementation as the non-private comparison arms, the paper's VAE and DP-VAE arms are adaptations of TVAE that swap mode-specific normalization for plain standardization, and CTGAN's mode-specific normalization is named in the introduction as an example of a preprocessing step that must itself satisfy differential privacy.
evidence: the baseline-models paragraph states that for CTGAN and TVAE the authors used the implementation from the Synthetic Data Vault project, footnote 3 giving github.com/sdv-dev/CTGAN, and that the non-DP baselines are CTGAN, TVAE and a VAE described as an adaptation of TVAE using a standardized preprocessing technique for the numerical columns, with DP-VAE adapted from that VAE under SmartNoise preprocessing; the introduction states that proposed improvements like mode-specific normalization introduced in Xu et al. must also satisfy DP because preprocessing steps themselves can impact privacy; section 5.1.2 credits the evaluation metrics including ML Efficacy to prior work naming Xu et al. 2019; the results tables report CTGAN, TVAE and VAE at epsilon infinity and DP-CTGAN and DP-VAE at epsilon 1 and 8 on Adult, Airline and Texas. Importance 4 rather than the MTabGen precedent's 3: beyond running the sdv-dev implementation as a baseline, two further comparison arms are built by modifying TVAE's preprocessing, and CTGAN's mode-specific normalization is part of the paper's motivating argument.

title: Evaluating Inter-Column Logical Relationships in Synthetic Tabular Data Generation
summary: Argues that the usual fidelity and utility measures miss whether a synthetic table preserves the logical relations that hold between its columns, and proposes three metrics for them - hierarchical consistency across nested geographic or organizational fields, mathematical and temporal dependency, and a distribution similarity index - then applies them to five generators on a real supply-chain dataset, finding that the latent-space models score well on distributional measures while failing the logical ones. CTGAN is one of the five evaluated generators, standing for the GAN category alongside SMOTE, TabDDPM, TabSyn and GReaT, and is reported across all the density, coverage, precision-recall and logical-consistency columns.
evidence: the introduction credits Xu et al. 2019 with proposing a GAN variant that learns the joint distribution through a minimax game, rendered by pypdf as GTGANs, and argues it fails to capture explicit conditional dependencies; section 3 names the five representative methods selected for the experiments as SMOTE, CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019), TabDDPM, TabSyn and GReaT, each generating about 140,000 samples from the DataCo supply-chain dataset over ten repeated runs; Table 1 reports CTGAN's density estimation, correlation, coverage, alpha-precision, beta-recall and hierarchical consistency scores, and the discussion groups CTGAN with TabDDPM and TabSyn as latent-space models that are reliable distributionally but struggle with inter-column logic. Importance 3: a compared generator among five, with none of CTGAN's machinery adopted.

title: Flexible Counterfactual Explanations with Generative Models
summary: Introduces counterfactual templates that let a user name which features may change at inference time rather than fixing the mutable set when the explainer is trained, and implements them in a generative adversarial explainer that also works black-box by learning from a historical prediction dataset instead of the classifier's internals, improving counterfactual validity over optimization-based benchmarks on economic and healthcare tables. CTGAN is the foundation the model is built on: its generator and discriminator architectures serve as FCEGAN's, its training-by-sampling supplies the real counterfactuals used in the discriminator loss, and an independently trained CTGAN discriminator is the paper's fakeness metric.
affiliations: Vrije Universiteit Brussel; University of Antwerp
evidence: appendix A states that the generator and discriminator of the Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) serve as the foundation for FCEGAN, including the independent CTGAN discriminator used for assessing fakeness, with residual layers in the generator and a PacGAN discriminator; the introduction states that FCEGAN incorporates techniques from CTGAN including training-by-sampling together with WGAN-GP to mitigate mode collapse; the loss section states that the real counterfactuals compared against by the discriminator loss are selected using the training-by-sampling method described in CTGAN; Table 1 defines the fakeness quality measure as D_CTGAN applied to the counterfactual. The compared benchmarks are counterfactual-search methods, not generators, so CTGAN is the substrate throughout rather than a baseline.

title: How Well Does Your Tabular Generator Learn the Structure of Tabular Data?
summary: Argues that tabular generative models are judged by criteria imported from image and text modalities and proposes structural fidelity - the alignment of causal structure between real and synthetic tables - as a fourth evaluation dimension alongside density estimation, downstream utility and privacy, then benchmarks nine generators from eight method families over seven datasets and reports that no single generator is strong on all four. CTGAN and TVAE are the GAN and VAE entries in that panel, and the benchmark's downstream-utility dimension is the train-on-synthetic test-on-real protocol adopted from Xu et al., which the paper also names as one of the inherited criteria it argues is insufficient on its own.
evidence: the introduction lists the evaluation dimensions mainstream benchmarks adopt from homogeneous modalities as density estimation, downstream utility citing Xu et al. 2019, and privacy preservation, and argues they fail to assess structural information; section 2.4 states that for all downstream tasks the authors adopt the train-on-synthetic test-on-real strategy citing Xu et al. 2019; section 2.6 lists the nine benchmark generators across eight categories, with TVAE (Xu et al. 2019) among the two VAE-based methods and CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) as the GAN method; the results tables report CTGAN and TVAE on density, alpha-precision, beta-recall, accuracy, RMSE, DCR, authenticity and local and global independence for both classification and regression datasets, and the per-generator radar figures include panels for each. Importance 3: two of nine benchmarked generators plus an adopted evaluation protocol, with no reuse of the conditional vector or mode-specific normalization.

title: Exponential Family Variational Flow Matching for Tabular Data Generation
summary: Extends variational flow matching to mixed-type tables by writing the per-feature posterior as a general exponential family distribution, which turns the training objective into moment matching and so covers continuous and discrete columns in one principled form, and relates the resulting objective to generalized flow matching under Bregman divergences before evaluating the model on the standard tabular benchmark suite. CTGAN and TVAE are the GAN and VAE baselines in that suite, reported on shape and trend error rates, alpha-precision, beta-recall and machine-learning efficiency across six datasets.
evidence: the baselines paragraph names the GAN-based comparator citing Xu et al. 2019, rendered in the PDF as CTAGAN, alongside VAE-based, diffusion and flow alternatives; Tables 1 and 2 report Shape and Trend error rates for CTGAN and TVAE against GOGGLE, TabDDPM, TabSyn, TabDiff and TabbyFlow on Adult, Default, Shoppers, Magic, Beijing and News; Table 3 and Table 4 rank CTGAN and TVAE on alpha-precision and beta-recall, and Table 8 reports their machine-learning efficiency AUC and RMSE against real data. Importance 3: compared generators only, with no reuse of the conditional vector or mode-specific normalization.

title: Reinforcement-Guided Hyper-Heuristic Hyperparameter Optimization for Fair and Explainable Spiking Neural Network-Based Financial Fraud Detection
summary: Combines a cortical spiking network with population coding and a reinforcement-guided hyper-heuristic search over its hyperparameters for detecting fraudulent bank account applications, targeting accuracy alongside group fairness and explainability, and evaluates it on the six bias variants of the Bank Account Fraud suite against gradient-boosted and prior spiking baselines under a reward that trades predictive equality against parameter count. CTGAN is the generator that produced the benchmark this work runs on: the paper records that the Bank Account Fraud suite was synthesized with it to preserve applicant anonymity, and states explicitly that CTGAN belongs to the dataset's creation and not to its own training pipeline.
evidence: section 4.1.1 states that the BAF Dataset Suite is a fairness-oriented benchmark of six variations drawn from real-world online bank account applications and that synthetic data was generated using a generative adversarial network to preserve client anonymity; the software paragraph in section 4 lists CTGAN, cited to Xu et al. 2019, among the libraries employed, as used in the original dataset generation; the Rationale for No Augmentation note states that the only data augmentation in the pipeline refers to CTGAN being used to generate the BAF dataset itself, not the authors' training process, and that synthetic oversampling such as SMOTE was deliberately avoided to preserve the 1.1% fraud rate. The tight scan returns two hits in the whole PDF, both accounted for here; there is no results row for CTGAN because it was never run by these authors.
needs: no convention covers this shape. The paper never runs CTGAN, yet every row it trains and evaluates on is CTGAN output, produced by the third-party Bank Account Fraud dataset authors. Recorded citation_only importance 2 as the conservative reading of the existing scale (CTGAN described, not run). The alternative is `inherited`, whose definition - SDV arrived inside a vendored third party rather than by a decision to embed it, and the intermediary is usually an index entry in its own right - fits closely if it is read to cover a third-party dataset as well as a vendored library, with the BAF suite as the intermediary entry. Importance would then plausibly be 3 rather than 2, since the paper's entire empirical substrate is CTGAN output. Needs a ruling before other dataset-inheritance cases are judged.
